title: Portuguese Woman
region: France (artist's nationality; place of making not stated on the page)
altText: A very large abstract painting made of patches and bands of color. The title says it shows a woman, but the image is built mainly from shapes and color rather than a detailed portrait.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil and wax painting on canvas by Robert Delaunay, made in 1916 and held by the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Spain. The art site lists it as a painting tagged Women, and lists two dimensions of 180 cm and 205 cm.

descriptions.k: This big painting is made of many bright colors and shapes. The title says it shows a woman. Look for curved shapes and patches of color. What colors can you find?
descriptions.g12: Robert Delaunay made this painting in 1916. It is full of bright colors and curved shapes, and the title says it shows a Portuguese woman. It is very large. Look for places where colors meet. What shapes do you see? Where might the woman be?
descriptions.g35: Robert Delaunay painted Portuguese Woman in 1916 with oil and wax on canvas. It is a very large painting, about two meters across, made of strong patches of color. The title tells us it shows a woman, but the shapes hint at her more than they draw her. Look at how colors meet. How does color build the picture?
descriptions.g68: Delaunay's Portuguese Woman (1916) is an oil-and-wax painting now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Spain. The art site labels it De Stijl, but Delaunay is more often linked with Orphism, a style that built paintings from contrasting colors. The title points to a woman, yet the canvas is organized by color and shape. How does Delaunay make color do the work of drawing?
descriptions.g910: Portuguese Woman (1916) is a large oil-and-wax painting by Robert Delaunay, held at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum. Delaunay is generally associated with Orphism, which treated color contrast as the basis of a picture, although the art site labels this work De Stijl. The title names a woman, but the surface is organized as color. How do figure and abstraction work together, and what is gained or lost by naming the subject?
descriptions.g1112: Delaunay's Portuguese Woman (1916), in oil and wax and now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, sits between portrait and abstraction. Delaunay is generally linked with Orphism, which made color relationships the main structure of a painting, though the art site files this work under De Stijl. The title anchors the canvas to a human subject while the surface resists description. How does the painting negotiate that tension, and what does the title add to your reading?

k.daily: Look at the big colorful shapes. Which shape do you like best?
k.emotion: The colors in this painting are bold. Do they make you feel loud or quiet?
k.observation: Look for a shape that might be a woman. Where do you think she is?
k.analysis: Find a place where two colors touch. Which two colors are they?
k.line: Trace one curved edge with your finger. Where does your finger go?
k.shape: Find a circle or a curved piece. Show me where it is.
k.color: Pick your favorite color in the painting. Where do you see it?
k.texture: This painting uses oil paint and wax. How do you think it would feel to touch?
k.space: This is a very big painting. Would you stand close or far away to see it? Why?
k.light: Which part looks brightest, like it is glowing?
k.meaning: The title says Portuguese Woman. What do you think she might be like?
k.culture: The title names a woman from Portugal. What is one thing you know about another country?
k.technique: The painter made big patches of color. Where do you see a patch that looks flat?
k.personal: If you were a color in this painting, which one would you be?
k.critical: Does this painting look like a real woman, or a made-up picture of shapes? Tell what you see.

g12.daily: How could you find the woman hidden among all the colors and shapes?
g12.emotion: What feeling do the strong colors give you? Tell why.
g12.observation: List three different colors you find and tell where each one is.
g12.analysis: Which part of the painting do your eyes visit first, and what makes them go there?
g12.line: Where do you see curved lines and where do you see straight ones? How are they different?
g12.shape: Which shapes seem to repeat in the painting, and where do they appear?
g12.color: Which colors sit next to each other and look very different? Tell how they look together.
g12.texture: This painting uses oil paint mixed with wax. How might that change how the surface looks?
g12.space: This painting is about as tall as a grown-up. How would it feel to stand in front of it?
g12.light: Which colors seem to glow, and which seem darker? What makes you say so?
g12.meaning: Why do you think the painter named this a woman if it is full of shapes?
g12.culture: Robert Delaunay was from France, and this painting names a woman from Portugal. What might a title tell you about a place?
g12.technique: How did the painter use patches of color instead of drawing small details?
g12.personal: What kind of music or sound would you match with this painting?
g12.critical: What would you change if you wanted the woman to be easier to see?

g35.daily: How does Delaunay mix a human figure and a pattern of color in this painting, and where do you see each?
g35.emotion: What energy do the bright, interlocking color areas give the painting, and which details help create it?
g35.observation: Describe where you can find the shapes that suggest the woman, and how you decided they belong to her.
g35.analysis: How do the groups of color and shape divide the canvas, and where does the painter create focus?
g35.line: How do curved edges and angled edges guide your eye across this large canvas?
g35.shape: Which shapes seem to belong to the figure, and which seem to belong to the background? How do they connect?
g35.color: How do contrasting colors placed side by side make each other look stronger?
g35.texture: The medium is oil and wax. What might the wax add to the look of the painted surface?
g35.space: The painting is about two meters wide and high. How might its size change the way viewers feel in front of it?
g35.light: How does Delaunay make color itself seem like a source of light?
g35.meaning: Why might an artist choose to hint at a woman instead of painting every detail of her face and clothes?
g35.culture: The title names a Portuguese woman. What can a title like this tell you about what an artist wants us to think about?
g35.technique: What challenges might the painter face when covering such a big canvas with controlled color shapes?
g35.personal: Which area would you want to look at longest, and what do you notice there?
g35.critical: How much does the title help you understand this painting, and what can you enjoy without it? Use details to explain.

g68.daily: How does the painting balance the idea of a recognizable woman with an abstract pattern of colors?
g68.emotion: How do the color combinations contribute to a mood of energy, rhythm or movement?
g68.observation: Which areas of the painting suggest a figure, and which seem purely abstract? How do you tell them apart?
g68.analysis: How do repeated shapes and color groups create a sense of unity across the large canvas?
g68.line: How do curving and angled boundaries between color areas suggest movement?
g68.shape: How do overlapping and interlocking shapes build both a figure and a pattern?
g68.color: How do complementary or strongly contrasting colors create vibration at the places where they meet?
g68.texture: How might the combination of oil and wax affect the way the color areas look and reflect light?
g68.space: How does Delaunay suggest depth with flat areas of color instead of traditional perspective?
g68.light: How does the arrangement of light and dark colors create a sense of glow without a single light source?
g68.meaning: This work is usually grouped with Orphism, which treated color as the main subject. How does the painting show that idea?
g68.culture: Delaunay painted in 1916, during World War I. How might that time shape what viewers see in a bright, rhythmic painting?
g68.technique: How does using color contrast in place of line and shading change what a painting can do?
g68.personal: What parts of your own world could you turn into color and shapes, and how would you do it?
g68.critical: Is it more important for viewers to recognize the woman or to experience the color? Defend your view with evidence.

g910.daily: How does the painting hold figuration and abstraction in tension, and what evidence in the shapes supports your answer?
g910.emotion: How does the rhythmic arrangement of color generate affect without relying on facial expression or narrative?
g910.observation: Examine the boundaries between color areas. What do they reveal about how the figure is built from the surface?
g910.analysis: How does the composition use repetition and variation to organize such a large field of color?
g910.line: How do edges, rather than drawn outlines, define direction and structure in the painting?
g910.shape: How do fragmented forms carry traces of the figure while remaining independent shapes?
g910.color: How does simultaneous contrast function as the painting's main structural tool?
g910.texture: How might the oil-and-wax medium shape the physical presence of color on the surface?
g910.space: How does Delaunay replace linear perspective with color relationships as the means of organizing space?
g910.light: How does the painting treat light as a property of color and not of illumination from a source?
g910.meaning: Delaunay is associated with Orphism. How does this painting argue that color alone can carry the structure of an image?
g910.culture: What does a title naming a particular national identity do for an abstracted figure, and what assumptions might it invite?
g910.technique: How does the painting's scale and the artist's color method demand a different kind of looking than a detailed portrait would?
g910.personal: What does this painting make you reconsider about what it means to recognize a person in an image?
g910.critical: Some sources label this work with a different movement than Orphism. Why might the categories used for abstract painting be contested?

g1112.daily: How does the painting use fragmentation of the figure to question the boundary between portrait and pure color structure?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the painting's energy come from color relations rather than from the sitter's character?
g1112.observation: Where does the figure resolve into recognizable parts and where does it dissolve? What does that pattern suggest about the painter's aims?
g1112.analysis: How do the compositional rhythms organize the surface while still allowing a reading of the subject?
g1112.line: How does the replacement of contour by color boundary relate to Delaunay's broader pursuit of a nonlinear painting?
g1112.shape: How do the interlocking planes function both as the body of the figure and as independent abstract elements?
g1112.color: How does the painting's theory of color contrast translate into a visual structure you can analyze?
g1112.texture: What might the choice of oil with wax suggest about the physical and experimental dimension of the painting?
g1112.space: How does color construct a flattened yet active space that departs from Renaissance perspective?
g1112.light: How does the painting reimagine light as pure chromatic relation, and how does that depart from Impressionist treatments of light?
g1112.meaning: How might Delaunay's Orphist emphasis on color as a language complicate the idea that a painting needs a recognizable subject?
g1112.culture: How might the context of 1916, the title's national identity and Delaunay's own position as a French painter shape the way we read the woman and the abstraction?
g1112.technique: What assumptions about skill and craft does a large abstracted figure built from color challenge, and which does it confirm?
g1112.personal: How does your own habit of searching for a recognizable image shape the way you look at this painting?
g1112.critical: How would you evaluate an argument that this painting is more an exploration of color theory than a portrait, and what evidence would you require?

teacherNote.context: A large oil and wax painting made in 1916 by Robert Delaunay, now in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Spain. Delaunay is generally linked with Orphism, which used color contrast as the main structure of a painting.
directions: Show students that a title can guide viewing. Ask them to search the painting for the woman and then explain how they decided.
Have students make a collage from colored paper in which a person or place is suggested only by patches of color.
Ask older students to compare this painting with Delaunay's Eiffel Tower with Trees and discuss how his treatment of a figure differs from his treatment of a landmark.
